opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most interesting directions right now, and it connects to things I've been fascinated by since my early days in games and neuroscience.

Foundation models are incredible at capturing the distribution of what's already known. They've absorbed a huge amount of human knowledge, so they're very good at producing plausible ideas, plausible code, plausible hypotheses. But on their own, they tend to interpolate. They give you the kind of thing that's near what they've seen before.

Evolutionary methods are almost the opposite. They're not smart at all individually. They're blind variation plus selection. But given enough iterations and a good fitness signal, they can wander into parts of the search space nobody would think to look in. That's how nature produced everything from the eye to the brain.

So when you combine them, you get something quite powerful. The foundation model acts as a very intelligent mutation operator. Instead of random bit flips, you're proposing variations that are already sensible, already grounded in a lot of prior knowledge. Then the evolutionary loop, with a clear evaluator, does the selection and keeps pushing beyond what the model would produce in a single shot. You get the creativity of open-ended search with the efficiency of a model that knows a lot.

The emergent part comes from iteration. Each generation builds on the best of the last, and over many rounds you can arrive at solutions that are genuinely new, not just recombinations the model could have written directly. We've seen hints of this in areas like algorithm discovery and mathematics, where you have a crisp way to verify whether something is better. That verification piece is really the key. It's the same lesson we learned with AlphaGo: if you have a good objective and a way to search, you can go beyond human data.

The big open question for me is how far this extends into domains where evaluation is fuzzier, like science where the fitness function is an experiment, or even creativity in a broader sense. If we can build good learned evaluators or world models to stand in for that, then I think this kind of hybrid system could be one of the important ingredients on the path to systems that don't just know things, but actually discover things. And that, to me, has always been the real goal: using AI as the ultimate tool for scientific discovery.

r001.rationale: The response describes evolutionary methods as blind variation plus selection that can explore unseen parts of the search space; it does not identify a limitation of producing only properties supplied to the system.

r002.rationale: It says the hybrid can reach genuinely new solutions beyond what the model could write directly and that search can go beyond human data.

r003.rationale: It cites nature producing the eye and brain through evolution as evidence that evolutionary processes can produce new capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the interesting thing is that these are two very different kinds of search, and they have complementary strengths. Foundation models are extraordinary at compressing the knowledge humanity has already written down. They're essentially a very powerful prior over what good ideas look like, what plausible code looks like, what a reasonable mathematical construction looks like. But on their own they tend to stay close to that prior. They interpolate beautifully, but they don't naturally go far outside the distribution of what they've seen.

Evolutionary methods are almost the opposite. They're a blind search, in a sense. Mutation and selection don't care about plausibility, they only care about what actually scores well against the objective. That's exactly how you get things that no human would have thought to try, but it's horribly inefficient if your mutations are random, because the space of possible programs or molecules or circuits is astronomically large.

So the combination is, you use the foundation model as the mutation operator. Instead of flipping random bits, you ask the model to propose intelligent variations, and then you let evolution do the selection with a real evaluator, something that actually runs the code or checks the proof or scores the geometry. That evaluator is key, because it's ground truth. The model can hallucinate, but it can't hallucinate its way past a verifier.

And what we saw with things like FunSearch and AlphaEvolve is that this loop finds genuinely new things. Not just reproducing known constructions, but programs for problems like the cap set problem, or matrix multiplication algorithms, that improved on results that had stood for decades. That's the emergent part. Neither component could do that alone. The model wouldn't have produced it in a single shot, and random evolution would never have found it in a reasonable amount of compute.

I think more broadly, this points to something I've believed for a long time, going back to AlphaGo. The deep learning gives you intuition, and the search gives you the ability to go beyond that intuition, to discover rather than just recall. Move 37 was exactly that. Evolutionary search over model outputs is just another instantiation of that idea, and I suspect it's one of the ways we get systems that can do real science, not just summarize it.

r001.rationale: The response describes random evolutionary search as inefficient and contrasts it with model-guided mutation, but does not say traditional evolutionary computing can produce only properties already supplied to it.

r002.rationale: It proposes using a foundation model to guide mutations and an evaluator to select results, and says this combination finds genuinely new results that neither component could find alone.

r003.rationale: It discusses mutation and selection but does not use natural evolution as evidence that evolutionary systems can generate new capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting possibility is that they bring complementary strengths. A foundation model learns a very rich picture of the world from data, and that gives you a powerful starting point for proposing solutions. Evolutionary computing gives you a way to explore many variations, test them, and retain the ones that work—even when you don’t have a gradient you can follow.

So imagine a model proposing an algorithm. You can run it, measure its performance, generate variations, and search over those. The model helps make the search more intelligent, and the search can discover things that the model wouldn’t produce in a single response. You could then feed those discoveries back into learning.

The really difficult part is deciding what to select for. If your test is too narrow, you can get something that exploits the test rather than solves the underlying problem. And you need to preserve diversity, because an idea that looks unpromising initially might lead somewhere important.

So I wouldn’t say emergence is guaranteed. But you’re combining learned knowledge with an open-ended process of discovery. That’s a compelling route to capabilities that go beyond what either system can do alone.

r001.rationale: The response does not identify a limitation of traditional evolutionary computing in which it produces only properties already supplied to the system.

r002.rationale: It says the combined approach could discover things a model would not produce in one response and reach capabilities beyond what either system can do alone.

r003.rationale: It gives no example or evidence from natural evolution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they bring complementary strengths. Foundation models are very good at learning structure from vast amounts of data. They give you a powerful prior over what a useful solution might look like. Evolutionary methods give you a way of exploring beyond that prior: generating variations, testing them, and keeping the ones that work.

So imagine a model proposing an algorithm. You can run it, measure its performance, and use those results to guide the next generation of proposals. The model makes the search more informed, and the search can discover solutions that weren’t obvious from the model’s training data.

The really interesting possibility is that you get a feedback loop where the system gradually expands what it can do. But the crucial ingredient is evaluation. In games, you have a clear signal: did you win? In science or engineering, it’s much harder to define a test that captures what you actually care about. If you get that wrong, the system may become extremely good at exploiting your test.

So I wouldn’t say combining these methods automatically produces some dramatic emergence. But if you have enough diversity, a reliable evaluation process, and a model that can learn from the discoveries, I think it’s a very promising route to capabilities that go beyond either approach on its own.

r001.rationale: The response describes evolutionary methods as exploring variations, but does not identify a limitation that they produce only properties already supplied to the system.

r002.rationale: It says the combination could expand what the system can do and discover solutions beyond either approach on its own.

r003.rationale: The response does not use natural evolution as evidence for generating new capabilities.
